title: History of soil science

definition.text: How ideas about soil developed, starting from concepts built on Justus von Liebig's chemistry and refined by agricultural scientists in laboratories, greenhouses and small field plots.

facts.text: Early agricultural chemists held a balance-sheet theory: soil was a more or less static store of plant nutrients that crops used and that could be replaced.
These early workers rarely looked at soil below the depth of normal tillage.
Early geologists accepted the balance-sheet theory and described soil as disintegrated rock, such as granite, sandstone or glacial till, modified by weathering and shaped into landforms.
Many early soil surveyors were geologists, because only they had the field methods needed; they saw soils mainly as weathering products of geologic formations.
Surveys published before 1910 were strongly shaped by geological ideas, and those of 1910 to 1920 added refinements but stayed fundamentally geological.
The balance-sheet theory ruled the laboratory and the geological concept ruled field work; both were taught in many classrooms until the late 1920s.
Broader concepts came from Eugene W. Hilgard and George Nelson Coffey in the United States and from Russian soil scientists, but the data behind them came from soil survey field work.
The balance-sheet idea keeps some value today, though understanding soils goes well beyond removing nutrients in crops and returning them as manure, lime and fertilizer.

notes: The Fallou section of this page (S:30f31c4ace37 onward) is used in the Friedrich Albert Fallou founder entry rather than a separate section entry.

definition.text: The school led by V. V. Dokuchaev and N. M. Sibirtsev from 1870, which treated soils as independent natural bodies with their own properties.

facts.text: Before it, soil was seen as a product of physical and chemical changes in rock, a dead substrate from which plants take mineral nutrients.
Its workers saw each soil's unique properties as the result of a unique combination of climate, living matter, parent material, relief and time.
Instead of inferring properties from rocks or climate, they read the combined effect of all these factors in the soil's own morphology.
Requiring all soil properties to be considered together as one integrated natural body made a science of soil possible; the ideas are called revolutionary.
Americans learned of the work through K. D. Glinka's 1914 textbook in German and especially C. F. Marbut's English translation of 1927.
Some enthusiasts thought soil study could ignore geology and agricultural chemistry, but the new concept in fact made those sciences more useful.
Soil morphology gave a firm basis for grouping observations, experiments and experience into principles that predict how soils behave.

definition.text: The American adaptation of the Russian soil concept, led by C. F. Marbut, which put the individual soil profile ahead of external soil features and surface geology.

facts.text: Focusing on profiles made early soil scientists overlook how much soils vary even within a small area, which seriously reduced the value of their maps.
Emphasis on genetic profiles was so strong that material without one, such as recent alluvium, seemed not to be soil, and rock weathering was sharply separated from soil formation.
Marbut insisted that classification rest on morphology, not on theories of soil genesis, which he saw as ephemeral and dynamic.
His 1935 classification relied on a "normal soil", formed in equilibrium on a landscape where downward erosion keeps pace with soil formation.
After 1930, studies moved from single pits to trenches or series of pits, and soils were described by ranges of properties around a central concept instead of one typical profile.
In the 1930s soil formation was explained by loosely conceived regional processes such as podzolization, laterization and calcification.

definition.text: The shift, from about 1940, to treating soil formation as many interrelated physical, chemical and biological processes open to quantitative study.

facts.text: Hans Jenny's 1941 book Factors of Soil Formation: A System of Quantitative Pedology summarized many basic principles of modern soil science up to that date.
Since 1940 time has gained much more weight among the soil-forming factors, with geomorphology used to find how long material has undergone soil formation.
Advances in soil chemistry, physics, mineralogy and biology added new tools for studying soil formation.
Attention moved from gross attributes of the whole soil to the co-varying detail of its parts, down to grain-to-grain relationships.

definition.text: The move from the qualitative soil classifications of Marbut and of 1938 to the quantitative Soil Taxonomy built under Guy D. Smith.

facts.text: The classes of Marbut's system and the 1938 USDA system were described qualitatively, not in terms that different scientists could apply consistently.
Neither system linked its higher, genetically defined classes to the soil series used in US soil mapping.
A 1949 modification of the 1938 system fixed some flaws but showed that its concepts and principles needed reappraisal.
More than 15 years of work under Guy D. Smith produced a new system, made official for the US National Cooperative Soil Survey in 1965 and published in 1975 as Soil Taxonomy.
The Smith system was adopted in the United States and by many other nations for their own classification.

definition.text: The broadening of soil survey after 1950 from farming, ranching and forestry to information on how soils affect nonfarm uses.

facts.text: Before 1950 soil surveys served mainly farming, ranching and forestry.
Some states saw their value for highway planning by the late 1920s and put soil interpretations in highway engineers' manuals in the 1930s and 1940s.
Nonfarm uses of soil grew rapidly in the 1950s and 1960s, creating a great need for information on soils' effects on them.
This had an immense impact on soil survey, especially during the 1960s.

definition.text: The study of how burrowing and mixing by living things shapes soil, from Darwin's earthworm work to its re-evaluation by soil geomorphologists from the 1980s.

facts.text: Darwin first recognized the importance of bioturbation for soil processes and geomorphology, devoting his last scientific book to it.
In 1891 geologist Nathaniel Shaler extended Darwin's idea to soil disturbance by ants and trees.
Rudolf Richter coined the term bioturbation in 1952 for sediment structures made by living organisms; since the 1980s it has been widely used in soil and geomorphology.
There is now ample evidence for Darwin's conclusions, and in many areas burrowing biota are major agents of soil formation.

title: The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms
article: The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms

definition.text: Charles Darwin's 1881 book on earthworms, their habits and their part in forming and moving the soil.

facts.text: It was Darwin's last scientific book, published in October 1881, shortly before his death.
It was the first significant work on soil bioturbation, though the term itself entered the soil and geomorphic literature only a hundred years later.
It carried Darwin's recurring theme that gradual changes over long periods can have large and sometimes surprising consequences.
Darwin calculated that there were 53,767 earthworms per acre.
He concluded that worms matter through their part in decomposing rock, slowly denuding the land, preserving archaeological remains and improving soil for plant growth.
Darwin found worms drag leaves into their burrows by the most efficient end and show complex, flexible behaviour despite rudimentary sense organs.
It sold thousands of copies in its first few weeks.

title: On the Formation of Mould
article: The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms#Paper "On the Formation of Mould"

definition.text: Darwin's 1837 paper to the Geological Society of London on the role of earthworms in forming soil.

facts.text: At Maer Hall his uncle Josiah Wedgwood showed him ground where lime and cinders spread years before lay beneath a layer of loam, and suggested earthworms were the cause.
Darwin read the paper on 1 November 1837; William Buckland backed its publication as "a new Geological Power" but rejected Darwin's idea that chalkland formed the same way.
It appeared in the society's Proceedings in 1838 and, with a woodcut, in its Transactions in 1840.

title: Burial of objects by earthworms
article: The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms#Summary

definition.text: The slow sinking of surface objects, from stones to Roman ruins, as earthworms bring up earth from below and leave it as castings.

facts.text: Darwin estimated the earth brought up by worms from the burial rate of surface objects and by weighing castings produced over set times.
He spread broken chalk on a pasture near Down House in December 1842; it ended up buried 18 centimetres deep, a rate of 6 millimetres per year.
He found Stonehenge's outer stones partly buried and studied Roman ruins such as Abinger and Silchester, concluding that worms, dust and soil wash had buried them.
Rain and wind move castings downslope, while worms' humic acids and the stones they swallow help break down rock.

conflicts.note: Bioturbation § Research history (S:982a010f571d) says the chalk was excavated 30 years after it was laid; probably rounding.

definition.text: The year 2015, declared by the United Nations General Assembly on 20 December 2013 to raise worldwide awareness of soils.

facts.text: It aimed to show the importance of soils for food security, agriculture, climate change mitigation, poverty alleviation and sustainable development.
The FAO implemented it within the Global Soil Partnership, which planned a website, logo and activities while organizations worldwide held local events.
In the United States the USDA held a kick-off event and the Natural Resources Conservation Service marked it with monthly themes.
It closed at FAO headquarters on 4 December 2015, and the IUSS then proclaimed 2015–2024 the International Decade of Soils to continue its work.

title: World Soil Day
article: International Year of Soils#World Soil Day

definition.text: An annual day, 5 December, that celebrates the importance of soil in people's lives.

facts.text: The International Union of Soil Sciences proposed 5 December as World Soil Day in 2002.
The UN General Assembly designated the day in December 2013, when it also declared 2015 the International Year of Soils.
The Soil Science Society of America and the American Society of Agronomy invite the public to keep celebrating it every year.
The FAO runs the #WorldSoilDay hashtag and campaigns such as "Stop soil erosion, Save our future", with activities for students, farmers, teachers and others.

title: World Congress of Soil Science

definition.text: The International Union of Soil Sciences' conference, held every four years apart from a break for World War II.

facts.text: A congress advances soil science and its application and handles the society's business; only members may attend.
The 1st congress met in Washington, DC, in 1927 and the 2nd in Leningrad in 1930.
About 2000 members have attended each congress since the 15th, in Acapulco, Mexico.
Editions of the World Reference Base were launched at congresses: the first at Montpellier in 1998 and the fourth at Glasgow in 2022.
Until 2014 the IUSS President was named by the national society hosting the next congress.
The 23rd congress met in Nanjing, China, in 2026; the 24th is planned for Toronto in 2030.

notes: S:3bfe04103f30 ('Of the 18 congresses ...') is out of date: the same page lists 23 congresses held through 2026; not used.

title: World Soil Museum

definition.text: A museum in Wageningen, the Netherlands, that displays soil profile monoliths representing the world's major soil types.

facts.text: It is managed by ISRIC, an independent science-based foundation, on the campus of Wageningen University and Research Centre.
It began as the International Soil Museum at the request of UNESCO and the International Society of Soil Science, to support the FAO-UNESCO Soil Map of the World.
Some 80 monoliths are on display, with a much larger collection of some 1000 from over 70 countries kept in its repository.
Each monolith comes with site information, a horizon-by-horizon profile description and data on chemical and physical properties.
It shows examples of the 32 WRB Reference Soil Groups, a section on Dutch soils and soils much changed by long human use.

notes: S:163379b54530 says the museum was created in 1996, yet ISRIC, which manages it, was established in 1966 on the same ISSS and UNESCO recommendation (S:3f02cda1a320); the 1996 date may be a typo for 1966.

title: V.V. Dokuchaev Central Museum of Soil
article: V.V. Dokuchaev Central Museum of Soil

definition.text: A soil museum in Saint Petersburg, founded in 1902 by Vasily Dokuchaev.

facts.text: Dokuchaev, commonly called the father of soil science, began his large collection of soil samples in 1880.
It opened in 1904, a year after his death, as the first museum of soil science in the world.
It holds about 330 soil monoliths from the Arctic to New Zealand, and expeditions bring new ones every year.

title: Australian Society of Soil Science Incorporated
article: Australian Society of Soil Science Incorporated

definition.text: Australia's not-for-profit professional association for soil scientists and others concerned with managing the country's soils, publicly known as Soil Science Australia.

facts.text: It was founded in 1955 to advance soil science in professional, academic and technical fields, and adopted its public name in 2011.
An elected Federal Council governs its seven branches, and members can gain accreditation as Certified Professional Soil Scientists.
It holds a national conference every two years, jointly with the New Zealand Society of Soil Sciences every fourth year.
It co-hosted the 19th World Congress of Soil Science in Brisbane in 2010.

definition.text: A professional and scientific membership society that fosters the science and art of managing natural resources sustainably.

facts.text: Hugh Hammond Bennett and three others proposed it at a Chicago meeting on 11 November 1941, and its first minutes date from 16 February 1943.
It was formed in 1943 as the Soil Conservation Society of America and took its present name in 1987.
It publishes the bimonthly peer-reviewed Journal of Soil and Water Conservation.

conflicts.note: The lead gives 1945; the History section gives 1943, with minutes from February 1943.

title: German Soil Science Society

definition.text: Germany's non-profit society of soil science experts and others interested in the field, the Deutsche Bodenkundliche Gesellschaft (DBG).

facts.text: It was founded in Berlin in 1926 as a section of the International Soil Science Society and re-formed in Wiesbaden after the Second World War.
It has around 2000 members, with headquarters in Göttingen since 2012.
Its meeting every two years is the main forum in German-speaking countries for new findings in soil science.
Its journal is the Journal of Plant Nutrition and Soil Science, published with the German Society of Plant Nutrition.

notes: S:bed6bd9db5eb says 'bi-annual' while S:4e877ed2c9c4 lists meetings in 2013 and 2015, so the meeting is read as every two years.

definition.text: A long-term field study at Rothamsted set up to test how fertilizers and manures affect hay yields.

facts.text: Begun in 1856 at Rothamsted Research in Hertfordshire and monitored ever since, it is one of the longest-running experiments in modern science.
Its treatments changed the plant make-up and ecology of the 28,000 m² field, making it a resource for studying natural selection and biodiversity.
It showed how plant species richness, biomass and pH are related, and that ordinary field trials probably underestimate long-term threats such as soil acidification.
Its archive of soil and hay samples has been used to track atmospheric pollution, including nuclear fallout.

definition.text: The chemistry, especially organic chemistry and biochemistry, of agriculture.

facts.text: It often aims to preserve or raise soil fertility so as to keep or improve crop yields and crop quality.
Soil analysis looks at the mineral matter, which makes up most of the mass of dry soil, and at organic matter, including humic and fulvic acids.
Time-honoured organic fertilizers have largely given way to chemicals from mined phosphate rock and the Haber-Bosch process, which greatly raised crop production.
Its pesticides raise yields but can contaminate ground and water and harm species they were not aimed at.

title: Long-term agricultural experiments

definition.text: Field experiments run for decades, some for more than 100 years, to test the sustainability of farming practices from yield trends.

facts.text: Examples include the Park Grass Experiment at Rothamsted, the Morrow Plots (1876), Sanborn Field (1888), the Magruder Plots (1892) and Auburn's Old Rotation (1896).
Rothamsted showed grain yields can be sustained for almost 150 years in wheat and barley monocultures given organic or inorganic fertilizer every year.
Even so, there is abundant evidence that crop rotation and organic inputs are often beneficial.
The Haughley Experiment ran organic farming without outside nutrients; whether its yield decline came from soil nutrient depletion is disputed.
Nitrogen released from soil organic matter can hide a legume nitrogen shortfall for a decade or more, so short trials cannot prove sustainability.
The Old Rotation showed legume nitrogen ploughed in as green manure can balance nitrogen removed by harvests over the long term.
In 2017 Rothamsted began the Large Scale Rotation Experiment to study regenerative approaches such as no-till and crop rotation.

notes: S:c832f0470c4e dates the Park Grass Experiment to 1843; Rothamsted Research (S:ac6d34b2ea5b) gives 1843 for Broadbalk and 1856 for Park Grass, so the 1843 is likely a mix-up and is left out of the fact.

verification.title: A new Rothamsted long-term field experiment for the twenty-first century: principles and practice

definition.text: A long-running field experiment at Rothamsted Research, sown with winter wheat every year since 1843.

facts.text: It is one of the classical field experiments begun by Lawes and Gilbert that remain in place as a resource for agricultural and environmental research.
Its continuous wheat showed take-all disease building up to a peak in the 3rd to 5th crop, then declining and restoring yields to 80 to 90% of early levels.

definition.text: Nikita Khrushchev's 1953 plan to boost Soviet farm output by ploughing new land in southern Western Siberia and northern Kazakhstan.

facts.text: After early success output fell considerably, and severe soil erosion made it an environmental disaster for the Kazakh steppe.
The region got only 200 to 350 mm of rain a year, mostly at harvest, and its soils had high salt content.
Strong winds blew snow off the fields in winter and caused soil erosion in spring.
Monoculture, with grain on 83% of cropland in 1958–1959, depleted the soil of nutrients.

definition.text: The world soil map published by FAO and UNESCO from 1971 to 1981 in 10 volumes at a scale of 1:5 million.

facts.text: The FAO soil classification was first developed as the map's legend and then applied by United Nations projects.
A Revised Legend of the Soil Map of the World followed in 1988.
The 3,230,000 km² of saline land worldwide has been mapped by region from it.
The World Soil Museum was created in 1996 at the request of UNESCO and the International Society of Soil Science to support it.

conflicts.text: Greyzem says the FAO classification was introduced with the UNESCO Soil Map of the World in 1978.
conflicts.note: FAO soil classification (S:de4d98df6761) gives 1974 for the map's first publication of the classification.

definition.text: The once-prevalent view that decayed plant matter, humus, was plants' main source of carbon.

facts.text: Fertilizers were believed to work by breaking humus down so plants could absorb it more easily.
Albrecht Thaer, a German agronomist, supported it and dismissed Humphry Davy's idea of atmospheric carbon.
The theory set out in Thaer's Principles of Agriculture (1809–12) was still accepted between 1800 and 1860.
Justus von Liebig argued against it.

title: Indian Institute of Soil Science

definition.text: An autonomous Indian research institute under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, set up for advanced research in soil science.

facts.text: Founded in 1988 at Bhopal, it covers coordinated projects on soil test crop response (17 centres), micronutrients and biofertilizers (11 centres each).

It has six divisions, among them soil physics, soil chemistry and fertility, soil biology and environmental soil science, and trains in soil testing, nutrient and water efficiency, carbon sequestration and soil quality assessment.

Its mandate covers research on soil physical, chemical and biological processes and environment-friendly management technologies; a long-term fertilizer experiments project studies fertilizer effects on productivity and soil quality.

notes: Institution summary; passes the navbox test; country-specific.

title: Central Soil Salinity Research Institute

definition.text: An autonomous Indian institute under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research for research on salt-affected soils.

facts.text: It began at Hisar in 1969 after an Indo-American team's water management recommendations and moved to Karnal that year.
Four divisions cover soil and crop management, irrigation and drainage engineering (groundwater recharge and subsurface drainage of waterlogged saline soils), crop improvement and social science.
Crop improvement breeds saline- and alkali-tolerant rice, wheat and mustard, and the institute coordinates the national project on managing salt-affected soils and using saline water.

notes: Institution summary; passes the navbox test; country-specific.

title: OPAL Soil Centre

definition.text: One of five centres of expertise of the Open Air Laboratories Network, based at the Centre for Environmental Policy, Imperial College London.

facts.text: It ran the OPAL Soil and Earthworm Survey, launched in March 2009, in which the public collected habitat and soil information and counted and identified earthworms.
Results were analysed to study soil and earthworm distribution across England and the effects humans have on soils.
Its aims include community-level information on soil quality and biodiversity, and research on pollution sources and pathways in soil.

notes: Citizen-science centre; passes the navbox test; country-specific.
